items.label: Nobody has counted New Testament variants.
items.subtitle: partial
items.haystack: nobody has counted new testament variants. peter gurry (nts 2016) estimates on the order of ~500,000 readings across the whole greek tradition — a extrapolation, not a hand count of every manuscript. our site does publish a mechanical count, but only for word-aligned disagreements vs sr gnt in extant letters of our 1–400 ce cntr witness slice — not the full ~5,700+ manuscript tradition. nobody-counted-variants partial

items.label: The New Testament text is completely unknown before late manuscripts.
items.subtitle: unsupported
items.haystack: the new testament text is completely unknown before late manuscripts. within our frozen window, substantial greek material survives from the second and third centuries (papyri) plus fourth-century codices such as 01 and 03. that does not recover every verse in every book from every century — but it falsifies the blanket claim that nothing early exists. nt-unknown-before-late unsupported

items.label: By about 400 CE the Greek New Testament text is largely recoverable.
items.subtitle: supported
items.haystack: by about 400 ce the greek new testament text is largely recoverable. standard critical-edition framing (and our site’s own scope statement) treats the fourth-century major codices plus earlier papyri as the backbone for reconstructing the greek text — while still not counting every later byzantine variant or replacing na28/ecm apparatus judgments. text-largely-recoverable-400 supported

items.label: P66, P75, 01, and 03 lack the Pericope Adulterae (John 7:53–8:11).
items.subtitle: supported
items.haystack: p66, p75, 01, and 03 lack the pericope adulterae (john 7:53–8:11). in cntr transcriptions in our corpus, that block is marked absent; narrative runs from 7:52 to 8:12 in those witnesses. later byzantine copies insert the pericope — a different story from our early slice. pa-absent-early supported

items.label: Mark originally ended at 16:8 in the earliest complete Greek codices in our window.
items.subtitle: supported
items.haystack: mark originally ended at 16:8 in the earliest complete greek codices in our window. codex sinaiticus (01) and codex vaticanus (03) end mark at 16:8 in the main greek tradition represented in cntr; the longer ending 16:9–20 is a later supplement in the manuscript record. textual critics still debate composition history — our data support the codex-level statement for 01/03. mark-ends-16-8 supported

items.label: The Comma Johanneum is in the earliest Greek tradition.
items.subtitle: unsupported
items.haystack: the comma johanneum is in the earliest greek tradition. 1 john 5:7–8 is extant in early greek witnesses with the short reading (spirit, water, blood). the explicit heavenly trinity wording of the comma is not attested in greek before the sixteenth century; it entered some latin lines and late greek retro-translations. comma-in-earliest-greek unsupported

items.label: The Lord’s Prayer doxology (“For thine is the kingdom…”) is in the earliest Alexandrian Greek…
items.subtitle: unsupported
items.haystack: the lord’s prayer doxology (“for thine is the kingdom…”) is in the earliest alexandrian greek witnesses of matthew. in cntr transcriptions for codex sinaiticus (01) and codex vaticanus (03), matthew 6:13 is extant but the greek ends at the petition against evil — the closing doxology familiar from the kjv is not part of that early line. later byzantine copies and liturgical tradition supplied the formula; na28/ubs5 omit it from matthew. lords-prayer-doxology-early unsupported

items.label: Acts 8:37 (the Ethiopian’s confession before baptism) is in our earliest Greek witnesses of A…
items.subtitle: unsupported
items.haystack: acts 8:37 (the ethiopian’s confession before baptism) is in our earliest greek witnesses of acts. cntr marks acts 8:37 absent (—) in codex sinaiticus, codex vaticanus, and 𝔓⁴⁵ within our 1–400 ce slice; the narrative runs from 8:36 to 8:38. the verse is common in byzantine copies and the textus receptus — a later expansion, not the earliest recoverable greek in our window. acts-8-37-early unsupported

items.subtitle: unsupported

items.label: The Qurʾān has no manuscript variation.
items.subtitle: unsupported
items.haystack: the qurʾān has no manuscript variation. the uthmanic text type is highly uniform, but published stemmatics (cook; sidky; van putten) report on the order of ~35–40 regional rasm differences among the four ʿuthmānic exemplar traditions — not wholesale content rewrites, but not zero graphic variation. early palimpsests such as ṣanʿāʾ 1 preserve a lower text that is not ut. quran-zero-variation unsupported

items.label: From about 650 CE the Uthmanic text type is already stable.
items.subtitle: supported
items.haystack: from about 650 ce the uthmanic text type is already stable. sidky and van putten’s archetype framing treats ut as stable from the seventh century onward for the rasm tradition they model — while allowing later scribal noise and regional graphic differences, not a claim of byte-identical copies everywhere. uthmanic-stable-650 supported

items.label: Early Qurʾān manuscripts show random independent spelling at each niʿmat allāh verse.
items.subtitle: unsupported
items.haystack: early qurʾān manuscripts show random independent spelling at each niʿmat allāh verse. van putten (bsoas 2019) collated fourteen early witnesses plus the cairo reference for niʿmat allāh / rabbi-ka: at nearly every attested verse they share the same ta vs ta marbūṭa choice as the 1924 rasm — including grammatically quirky pairings — with only isolated disagreements (e.g. q 16:114, q 37:57). that pattern fits a shared written archetype copied from exemplars, not independent invention at each verse. quran-nimat-random-spelling unsupported

items.label: Shared idiosyncratic spellings in early Uthmanic manuscripts support a written Uthmanic arche…
items.subtitle: supported
items.haystack: shared idiosyncratic spellings in early uthmanic manuscripts support a written uthmanic archetype. within scope of published collation work (van putten 2019; stemma framing in cook and sidky): when many early ut manuscripts agree on the same non-standard rasm at the same ayah — the niʿmat case is the site’s illustrative proof — the straightforward scholarly explanation is descent from a single written archetype and copying from written exemplars. that is early standardization of a text type, not a claim about zero variation (see regional rasm) or about proving ʿuthmān’s personal authorship. quran-shared-idiosyncrasies-archetype supported

items.label: The ~40 Uthmani regional rasm differences are the same thing as the Seven or Ten qirāʾāt.
items.subtitle: unsupported
items.haystack: the ~40 uthmani regional rasm differences are the same thing as the seven or ten qirāʾāt. cook/sidky’s ~35–40 graphic splits concern the four ʿuthmānic exemplar traditions within one written uthmanic text type — consonantal/orthographic stemmatics, not the later canonized reading lines (nasser; shah; van putten). qirāʾāt specify recitation atop rasm; they are related historically but not a one-to-one map to each regional rasm report. illustrative manuscripts publishes rasm tables only — no qirāʾāt census. quran-rasm-equals-qiraat unsupported

items.label: The Ṣanʿāʾ lower text proves the Uthmanic text is late fiction.
items.subtitle: partial
items.haystack: the ṣanʿāʾ lower text proves the uthmanic text is late fiction. sadeghi & goudarzi (2012) show the palimpsest’s lower layer is a non-uthmanic companion-era line with real divergences from standard ut rasm — important evidence for early textual diversity. that does not erase the separate manuscript record of ut-type hijazi copies, regional rasm stemmatics, or shared orthography arguments on this site. “late fiction” overstates what one palimpsest layer can disprove. sanaa-proves-uthmanic-fiction partial

items.label: Undotted early Qurʾān manuscripts mean any reading is equally original.
items.subtitle: partial
items.haystack: undotted early qurʾān manuscripts mean any reading is equally original. hijazi rasm is often written without full vowel pointing, so the consonantal line alone underdetermines pronunciation — that is why qirāʾāt scholarship exists. but underdetermination is not license to ignore transmission: early ut witnesses still show highly uniform rasm with patterned splits (cook/sidky) and shared idiosyncrasies (van putten 2019). undotted script invites reading traditions; it does not make every hypothetical reading equally attested. undotted-mss-any-reading-original partial

items.subtitle: unsupported
items.haystack: illustrative manuscripts proves intentional theological corruption at scale. optional intentional-vs-error tags on some greek nt units are heuristic and model-assisted — useful for exploration, not proof of motive across the tradition. most counted units are spelling, word order, or ordinary scribal difference vs sr gnt. proves-theological-corruption unsupported

items.subtitle: unsupported

items.label: Our niʿmat allāh matrix is a complete census proving the entire Qurʾān rasm never varied.
items.subtitle: unsupported
items.haystack: our niʿmat allāh matrix is a complete census proving the entire qurʾān rasm never varied. the shared-orthography page reproduces van putten 2019 table 2 for one published niʿmat/rabbi-ka case study — an illustration of shared written idiosyncrasies, not a generated variant census of all early manuscripts or all verses. regional rasm splits and ṣanʿāʾ palimpsest layers still show graphic diversity elsewhere. quran-nimat-full-census unsupported

items.label: Our census equals the NA28 apparatus or all Greek manuscripts.
items.subtitle: out of scope
items.haystack: our census equals the na28 apparatus or all greek manuscripts. out of scope by design: we mechanically align a bounded cntr witness set to sr gnt. na28/ecm/igntp record editorial judgments and thousands of witnesses beyond our 1–400 ce illustrative slice. census-equals-na28 out_of_scope

items.label: The Masoretic Text is identical to what Jesus read.
items.subtitle: partial
items.haystack: the masoretic text is identical to what jesus read. second-temple and pre-christian hebrew witnesses in our corpus (dead sea scrolls, nash papyrus) show a largely continuous consonantal tradition alongside spelling diversity and occasional longer or shorter readings in some books. that supports substantial continuity for much of the hebrew bible — not byte-identical identity with every medieval masoretic codex for every verse a first-century reader might have heard. mt-identical-jesus-read partial

items.label: The Septuagint is a late Christian invention.
items.subtitle: unsupported
items.haystack: the septuagint is a late christian invention. jewish greek torah and prophetic books are attested on pre-christian papyri in this site’s hebrew/lxx slice — e.g. p.ryl. 458 (genesis), p.fouad 266 (deuteronomy), p.oxy. 1007 (exodus) — centuries before christian recensions and church fathers. later christian copies and revisions exist; that is not the same as inventing the whole greek old testament tradition. lxx-late-christian-invention unsupported

items.label: 1QIsaᵃ proves the Bible never changed.
items.subtitle: partial
items.haystack: 1qisaᵃ proves the bible never changed. the great isaiah scroll agrees with the masoretic book of isaiah far more often than it disagrees — a key data point for stability. it also preserves thousands of spelling variants and documented textual differences elsewhere in the dss corpus; “remarkable agreement in isaiah” is not a license to claim zero textual history for the whole hebrew bible. 1qisa-proves-never-changed partial

items.label: The Old Testament survives only in medieval manuscripts — nothing earlier exists.
items.subtitle: unsupported
items.haystack: the old testament survives only in medieval manuscripts — nothing earlier exists. within our hebrew/lxx window, material survives from the second century bce onward (dss) and from pre-christian greek papyri. that does not recover every book on every leaf for every century — but it falsifies the blanket claim that no pre-medieval witnesses exist. ot-unattested-before-medieval unsupported

items.label: The Septuagint is irrelevant to New Testament authors — they only used Hebrew.
items.subtitle: partial
items.haystack: the septuagint is irrelevant to new testament authors — they only used hebrew. many nt citations and allusions follow greek old testament wording that matches the lxx (or a closely related greek tradition) more closely than a fresh translation from the medieval mt would — e.g. in matthew, hebrews, and pauline letters. that does not mean every ot echo is lxx-only, or that hebrew was unread in the second temple period. it does refute the blanket that lxx is irrelevant to how nt authors quote scripture in greek. lxx-irrelevant-nt-authors partial

items.label: Nag Hammadi texts are lost books of the New Testament canon.
items.subtitle: partial
items.haystack: nag hammadi texts are lost books of the new testament canon. the find shows how diverse early christian literature was — and some titles (e.g. gospel of thomas) overlap sayings also known from greek fragments. but these are fourth-century coptic codices of mostly gnostic tractates, not uncatalogued greek nt manuscript copies. church lists debated individual works; they were not treated as the same stream as matthew–revelation in the greek nt tradition this site collates (1–400 ce cntr). nag-hammadi-lost-nt-books partial
